A.explanation: The deformation cannot be both because returning along the same curve to zero extension leaves no permanent extension for plastic behaviour.

B.explanation: The sample does return to zero extension when force is removed, so it must show elastic behaviour between X and Y.

C.explanation: Plastic deformation would leave a residual extension at zero force, but the unloading curve returns to the origin.

D.explanation: The sample returns to zero extension along the same curve, so deformation between X and Y is recovered and is elastic with no plastic permanent set.

hints: Notice the shape of the force-extension graph: straight from 0 to X, then curved from X to Y, with unloading stated to follow the same curve back to the origin.
Recall that elastic means the extension becomes zero when the force becomes zero, while plastic means a permanent extension remains at zero force.
Check whether the curved X to Y section returns to zero extension and what that implies about Hooke's law versus elastic recovery.
walkthrough: Look at the given graph and statement: loading goes from 0 to X to Y, then unloading from Y retraces the same force-extension curve back to 0.
State the test for elastic behaviour: if $extension = 0$ when $force = 0$ after removal of load, the deformation is elastic because it is fully recovered.
State the test for plastic behaviour: if $extension > 0$ when $force = 0$ after removal of load, part of the deformation is permanent and plastic.
Apply this to the X to Y region: because the return path goes back through X to the origin, the extra extension gained between X and Y is removed when the force is removed.
Note the curve between X and Y is no longer straight, so $F$ is no longer proportional to $x$ there, but non-proportional deformation can still be fully recovered and therefore still elastic.
Hence between X and Y the metal shows recoverable deformation with no permanent set, which is elastic but not plastic. This is option D.
